title: Why Do We Want to Leave a Legacy?
metaTitle: Why Do We Want to Leave a Legacy? What Research Suggests
metaDescription: Wanting to leave a mark is a normal response to mortality and the need to matter. Here is what research on generativity and symbolic immortality suggests.
keyFinding: The urge to leave a legacy appears to be a normal, meaning-giving response to two deep human pulls — the wish to contribute to the next generation, and the wish to matter beyond our own lifespan.
honestAnswer: Wanting to leave a mark is not vanity or fear in disguise — it is one of the most well-documented ways humans make meaning, and most of the research treats it as a normal part of adult development rather than a problem to fix. Two related ideas explain most of the pull. One is the drive psychologists call generativity: the wish to care for, teach, and contribute to people who will outlive us. The other is the awareness, however quiet, that our time is finite, which seems to push us toward forms of contribution that will continue when we are gone.

Put simply, the desire for legacy tends to combine a forward-facing wish to give something to the future with a deeper wish to matter beyond our own span. Both are ordinary. The honest framing is that this impulse is widespread, tends to grow as we age, and — handled well — is associated with a fuller sense of purpose rather than with morbidity or ego.
whatDataShows: The clearest framework comes from Erik Erikson, who described generativity — caring for and contributing to the next generation — as a central task of midlife adulthood, set against its opposite, stagnation. In his model, the people who lean into mentoring, raising others, building, and contributing tend to experience that stage as meaningful, while those who do not can feel stuck or self-absorbed. Later researchers built measures of generativity and have linked higher generative concern with greater wellbeing and life satisfaction, though much of this work is correlational.

A second strand comes from Terror Management Theory, developed by Pyszczynski, Greenberg, and Solomon, which argues that awareness of our own mortality is a powerful, often unconscious motivator. One of its central claims is that humans pursue what the theory calls symbolic immortality — the sense of living on through children, work, ideas, communities, or impact — as a way of coping with the knowledge that we die. On this account, the wish for legacy is partly a response to mortality, channelled into something constructive.

These two ideas converge in research by Grant and Wade-Benzoni and colleagues suggesting that reminders of mortality, rather than only producing fear or avoidance, can heighten generative and prosocial motivation — the wish to help, give, and leave something worthwhile. The effects are nuanced and depend on framing, but the broad pattern points the same way: thinking about finitude can turn attention toward contribution.
whyItFeelsDifferent: Legacy can feel like an ego project — something only the famous or the wealthy are entitled to want — because the word conjures monuments, fortunes, and names on buildings. But in the research the impulse is far more ordinary and relational: raising a child, teaching a skill, mentoring a colleague, tending a community, or leaving work that helps someone you will never meet all count, and all seem to draw on the same generative drive.

It can also feel uncomfortable because it brushes up against mortality, which most of us prefer not to dwell on. If the wish to matter beyond our lifespan is partly fuelled by awareness that the lifespan ends, then noticing the wish can quietly remind us of the reason for it. That discomfort is part of why the impulse is easy to dismiss or rationalise rather than examine.

And because culture celebrates the grand, visible legacy, the small and slow kinds — the ones most people actually leave — can feel like they don't count. The research does not support that hierarchy. The mechanism appears to be the same whether the contribution is enormous or quiet.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most consistent suggestion from the generativity literature is to treat legacy as something you do now rather than something you arrange for later — mentoring, teaching, building, caring, and contributing in the present are exactly the behaviours associated with the meaning generativity is meant to provide. You do not have to wait for a deathbed plan; the drive is satisfied by ongoing contribution.

Where mortality awareness comes up — a milestone birthday, a loss, an illness in the family — the research suggests it can be channelled constructively rather than suppressed. Studies in the Terror Management and generativity traditions indicate that reflecting on finitude can increase the wish to give and connect; directing that energy toward something you care about tends to be more productive than either dwelling on the fear or pushing it away.

It also helps to define legacy in your own, relational terms rather than against a public scoreboard. Because the meaning seems to come from contribution itself, scaling the ambition to what is actually within reach — the people and work in front of you — is more likely to deliver the sense of purpose than measuring yourself against the rare, monumental version.
whatDoesNotHelp: Treating legacy as a status competition — bigger name, bigger fortune, bigger monument — tends to miss the point the research points to, which is that the meaning comes from generative contribution rather than from public scale. Chasing recognition can leave the underlying wish unsatisfied even when the recognition arrives.

Suppressing thoughts of mortality entirely does not appear to help either; the theory and supporting studies suggest the wish to matter is fuelled in part by that awareness, so refusing to acknowledge it can leave the drive unexamined and easy to misdirect rather than resolved.

Postponing all of it to a future plan — the will, the foundation, the someday project — overlooks the finding that generativity is something experienced through present action. Waiting to leave a legacy until the end can forfeit most of the meaning the impulse is there to provide.
realNumbersInContext: This is a topic where the honest currency is frameworks and patterns, not precise statistics, and the underlying research is largely correlational — so it is worth holding the conclusions loosely. The two anchoring ideas are Erikson's stage of generativity versus stagnation in midlife, and Terror Management Theory's concept of symbolic immortality. Neither yields a tidy number; both describe a direction of motivation that shows up widely.

What the studies do reasonably support is a pattern: generative concern tends to be associated with higher wellbeing, and reminders of mortality can — depending on how they are framed — increase generative and prosocial motivation rather than only fear. Read these as well-supported tendencies, not laws, and as evidence that the wish to leave a mark is normal rather than something to explain away.

faqs.question: Is wanting to leave a legacy selfish or egotistical?
faqs.answer: Research generally frames it as the opposite: the underlying drive, generativity, is about caring for and contributing to people who will outlive you. It can be expressed in ego-driven ways, but the core impulse — to give something to the future — is one of the more prosocial human motivations, and is linked with greater wellbeing rather than self-absorption.

faqs.question: Does the desire for legacy come from fear of death?
faqs.answer: Partly, according to Terror Management Theory, which argues that awareness of mortality pushes us toward symbolic immortality — living on through children, work, or impact. But it is not only fear: Erikson's idea of generativity describes a positive wish to contribute that develops in adulthood. Both strands likely contribute, and the effects depend on framing.

faqs.question: Do I need to do something big to leave a legacy?
faqs.answer: The research does not support that. Generativity is expressed through ordinary, relational acts — raising a child, mentoring, teaching, building, tending a community. The meaning appears to come from contribution itself, not from public scale, so small and slow legacies seem to draw on the same drive as grand ones.

faqs.question: Why does the wish to matter often grow as we get older?
faqs.answer: Erikson placed generativity as a central task of midlife, and mortality tends to feel more present with age, which Terror Management research links to a stronger pull toward contribution. So both the developmental clock and growing awareness of finitude point the same way, though this is a general pattern rather than a rule.

faqs.question: Is thinking about my legacy morbid?
faqs.answer: Not according to the research, which suggests reflecting on finitude can heighten the wish to give and connect rather than only producing dread. Channelled constructively, mortality awareness is associated with more generative, prosocial motivation. The discomfort is real, but it tends to point toward meaning rather than away from it.

dataSources: Erik Erikson — psychosocial stages of development; generativity versus stagnation as the central task of midlife adulthood.
Terror Management Theory (Pyszczynski, Greenberg, & Solomon) — mortality awareness and the pursuit of symbolic immortality.
Grant, A. M., & Wade-Benzoni, K. A. — work on death awareness and its effects on generative and prosocial motivation at work.
